reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: Polysplenia is the visceral hallmark of left atrial isomerism (bilateral left-sidedness), with multiple small spleens usually clustered along the greater curvature of the stomach.
Bilateral bilobed lungs with hyparterial bronchi and paired morphologically left atrial appendages are the defining thoracic features.
Interruption of the intrahepatic inferior vena cava with azygos or hemiazygos continuation is a characteristic and surgically important finding.
Cardiac lesions are typically less severe than in asplenia but commonly include atrioventricular septal defect, partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection and left-sided obstructive lesions.
Sinus node dysfunction and congenital complete heart block are frequent because the sinus node is hypoplastic, malpositioned or absent.
Extracardiac associations include intestinal malrotation, a midline symmetrical liver, and biliary atresia, the last carrying significant hepatic morbidity.
Despite multiple spleens, splenic function may be reduced, so immunisation status and splenic reserve should be assessed rather than assumed.
Some individuals with mild cardiac anatomy present in adulthood incidentally on imaging performed for unrelated reasons.
reference.pathophysiology: Polysplenia reflects a laterality defect in which the embryo fails to establish rightward differences and instead duplicates left-sided morphology on both sides of the body. Disruption of nodal cilia-driven leftward flow and the downstream Nodal-Lefty-Pitx2 pathway leads to bilateral 'left' patterning, so the lungs are both bilobed with hyparterial bronchi and the atrial appendages are both of morphologically left type. The spleen, normally a single left-sided organ, forms as multiple splenic nodules. Because the sinus node is a right-sided structure that fails to develop normally in bilateral left-sidedness, conduction is frequently abnormal with atrial rhythms or heart block. Interruption of the hepatic segment of the inferior vena cava occurs because the right-sided venous confluence does not form, and systemic venous return is rerouted through the azygos system. Associated abnormalities of gut rotation and of the biliary tree arise from the same failure of asymmetric organogenesis.
additionalDifferentials: accessory spleens or splenosis in situs solitus
isolated interrupted inferior vena cava with azygos continuation
additionalInvestigations: abdominal ultrasound demonstrating multiple splenic nodules and hepatic symmetry
echocardiography with attention to systemic and pulmonary venous drainage
cross-sectional imaging showing interrupted inferior vena cava with azygos continuation
twelve-lead ECG and ambulatory monitoring for sinus node dysfunction or heart block
peripheral blood film to assess functional splenic activity
hepatobiliary imaging where biliary atresia is suspected in infancy
genetic testing for laterality and ciliopathy genes in selected patients
redFlags: bradyarrhythmia, syncope or antenatally detected complete heart block
bilious vomiting or abdominal signs suggesting volvulus from malrotation
conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and pale stools indicating biliary atresia
signs of overwhelming infection where splenic function is impaired
progressive cyanosis or heart failure from evolving cardiac lesions
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally more favourable than right isomerism and depends on the complexity of the cardiac defect, the presence of heart block, and whether biliary atresia supervenes. Many patients achieve good long-term survival with staged cardiac repair, pacing where indicated, and vigilant management of hepatic and infective complications.
pitfalls: Assuming normal splenic immune function simply because multiple spleens are present.
Missing interruption of the inferior vena cava before catheterisation or cardiac surgery.
Overlooking evolving heart block that may be silent until syncope or fetal compromise.
Failing to investigate neonatal cholestasis for associated biliary atresia.
Not screening for intestinal malrotation, risking acute volvulus.
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
Radiological reviews of heterotaxy and situs anomalies
management: Staged surgical repair of the associated cardiac defects such as atrioventricular septal defect and anomalous pulmonary venous connection
Permanent pacing for sinus node dysfunction or congenital complete heart block
Assess splenic function and, where functional hyposplenism is present, give pneumococcal and other immunisations against encapsulated organisms with prophylactic antibiotics
Surgical correction of intestinal malrotation by a Ladd procedure, with vigilance for midgut volvulus
Timely management of biliary atresia by Kasai portoenterostomy, progressing to liver transplantation if hepatic failure supervenes
Electrocardiographic and ambulatory rhythm surveillance for evolving conduction disease
Paediatric cardiology-led multidisciplinary care coordinating cardiac, hepatobiliary and gastrointestinal management
